title: How emission reduction and commercial outcomes go hand in hand
summary: FuelEU Maritime and EU ETS are escalating compliance costs, forcing operators to integrate carbon management into commercial decisions. Industry discussions frame "emission savings" and FuelEU pooling as "commercial opportunities" to manage compliance surpluses. This system risks allowing ships exceeding carbon intensity targets to simply buy credits, enabling continued high emissions instead of mandating genuine decarbonisation for the dirtiest vessels.
content:
As maritime emissions regulation becomes increasingly complex, owners, operators and charterers face a growing challenge: understanding what carbon compliance means for their commercial decisions.

With the FuelEU Maritime and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) regulations already influencing economics, and further developments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) still under discussion, the cost of emissions can no longer be treated as a separate consideration. Fuel choices, operational efficiency and contractual arrangements are all playing an increasingly important role in determining the profitability of a voyage.

However, while the regulatory landscape presents challenges, it is also creating new commercial opportunities. Understanding the value of emissions savings, managing compliance surpluses and identifying opportunities to improve operational efficiency can help shipping companies turn decarbonisation into a business advantage.

These were among some of the key themes explored during a recent Baltic Exchange Emissions and Efficiency Update webinar, featuring Maximilian Schroer, Co-founder of BetterSea, Haris Zografakis, Senior Consultant at Stephenson Harwood and Executive Chairman of Blue Visby Services, and Martin Crawford-Brunt, Emissions Lead at Baltic Exchange.

A key distinction in the current regulatory landscape is the difference between EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime. As Schroer explained, companies must consider several questions when managing their FuelEU position, such as which fuel they choose, where should they consume it, how should they trade any resulting surplus, and who ultimately controls its value?

Pooling vessels

FuelEU pooling is an important part of this equation. It allows vessels that perform better than the required greenhouse gas intensity target to transfer their surplus compliance balance to vessels in deficit, helping them avoid penalties while potentially creating a revenue stream for surplus-generating vessels.

However, the value of that surplus depends on the cost of generating it, which varies considerably depending on the fuel choice. During 2025, BioLNG was the largest seller of compliance surplus and effectively set the market price. Although LNG offered a relatively low cost of surplus generation, much of the available surplus was banked by owners rather than sold. By 2026, the picture had changed, with Bio100 becoming the cheapest source of surplus generation.

BetterSea’s FuelEU index provides a daily reference price for compliance surplus, based on executed trades. The 2025 volume-weighted average was approximately €193 per tonne, but prices have since fallen, with the monthly average reaching around €120 in June and €84 in October. This reflects the potential commercial attractiveness of purchasing surplus rather than facing a compliance penalty.

The changing market also highlights the importance of understanding who is responsible for pooling. This depends on the contractual relationship, including whether a vessel is operated by its owner or on time charter, and the length of the charter period. Operators may focus on optimising buying and selling decisions within the reporting period, while owners with longer-term interests may wish to consider banking surplus for future use. In either case, charter parties need to reflect realistic market values, with index-based pricing helping to provide greater transparency and reduce the potential for disputes.

Waiting at anchorage

Regulation is only one part of the decarbonisation equation. Improving operational efficiency can also deliver significant commercial benefits, often without requiring a change of fuel or substantial investment in new technology.

Zografakis highlighted the inefficiency created when ships sail at speed, only to spend extended periods waiting at anchorage. This results in unnecessary fuel consumption, higher emissions and additional costs for both owners and charterers.

He noted that the ideal solution to this is by combining operational optimisation with a benefit-sharing arrangement between the parties. By adjusting sailing speeds and coordinating vessel arrival times with berth availability, vessels can reduce fuel consumption and time spent waiting at anchorage. Under the model discussed, the charterer compensates the owner for the additional time spent at sea, while fuel savings are shared between the parties, typically on a 50/50 basis, although this can be negotiated.

The approach aims to improve the financial position of both parties compared with a conventional voyage, with emissions reductions of approximately 10-18% as an additional benefit. The optimisation process accounts for vessel performance, contractual requirements, terminal schedules, berth availability and environmental conditions, including first-come, first-served port arrangements.

Baltic’s reliable benchmarks

The wider message is that emissions reductions and commercial performance do not have to be competing objectives. With the right contractual and operational arrangements, improved efficiency can create a financial benefit for both sides of a charter.

Understanding these opportunities requires reliable benchmarks and practical tools to translate regulatory requirements into financial terms. This is where the Baltic Exchange’s free emissions calculators have an important role to play.

Developed to help the market navigate the growing complexity of emissions regulation, the calculators allow users to compare the relative financial and environmental implications of different fuel and operational choices against Baltic standard ships and standard routes.

The FuelEU Maritime calculator allows users to select a vessel type and adjust key variables, including vessel size, speed, fuel consumption, fuel type and fuel prices. The results provide a comparison against a Baltic benchmark vessel operating on conventional very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO), helping users understand the potential impact on voyage costs.

The TCE calculator provides another practical commercial application, converting a lump-sum voyage calculation into a TCE figure that incorporates ETS and FuelEU impacts.

The calculators are designed to provide relative comparisons rather than absolute compliance assessments for individual vessels. By using a consistent market benchmark, they give owners, operators and charterers a common starting point for understanding the financial implications of different decisions and negotiating the allocation of costs and benefits.

Trusted reference points

As the industry becomes increasingly data-driven, commercial parties are still somewhat reluctant to share granular operational or financial data. Despite this, even where calculations can be automated, the market still needs trusted reference points when negotiating freight rates, compliance costs and the value of emissions savings.

Ultimately, maritime decarbonisation is moving beyond the initial ambition-setting phase. Regulation is creating direct financial consequences, while new approaches to pooling, fuel selection and operational efficiency are opening up commercial opportunities.

title: Frantic back-room haggling as climate deal for global shipping goes down to the wire
summary: The IMO's "frantic haggling" over a Net-Zero Framework (NZF) and global carbon pricing reveals deep-seated resistance to meaningful climate action from certain states. Despite warnings against watering down the NZF, ongoing compromises, influenced by opponents like the US and Saudi Arabia, risk allowing continued high carbon intensity. This dithering directly enables continued reliance on heavy fuel oil, ensuring many vessels will keep exceeding their CII ratings and evade truly impactful carbon pricing penalties.
content:
Over 120 governments are frantically trying to reach a compromise on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a historic climate agreement that would introduce the world’s first global carbon pricing, at the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London.

This week has been the technical negotiations (ISWG-GHG-23) on 23-27 November. The IMO meets next week for decisive political negotiations (MEPC 85), on 30 November – 3 December, and (unlikely) the Extraordinary Session (MEPC E.2) on 4 December if the room is ready to adopt.

Delegates met in the working group on Monday and in closed, informal discussions throughout the week, led by Japan and co-facilitated by Brazil, Canada, the European Commission, Ireland, Norway and China, to work towards consensus on the NZF’s key elements: the agreed limits to phase-out fossil fuels, clean energy and the carbon pricing revenues. The informal discussions are referenced in the outcome report of the meeting and are set to continue next week.

Delegates observed that the majority of countries engaged constructively in the informal discussions to preserve the ambition in the NZF, with its opponents (US, Saudi Arabia and fellow petro states) looking increasingly isolated.

Experts warn any further compromises that would water down the NZF’s elements would put at jeopardy the industry’s clean transition as well as vulnerable countries, and it would move the IMO even further away from achieving its own 2023 Revised Strategy commitments. Economic analysis by RMI + UCL says that the NZF is the best, most cost-effective policy tool amidst other alternatives to achieve the IMO’s own target: reaching net-zero by/around 2050 in an equitable way.

The NZF remains on the table and it is the most mature policy package that can be adopted next week.

Why this matters: Decisions at the IMO will decide the fate of ~5% of global oil demand represented by global shipping, responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually. Governments at the IMO committed to decarbonise the sector on a pathway consistent with the Paris Agreement’s safe temperature goals.

Failing to agree on a global regulation for shipping would likely lead to a patchwork of national and regional regulation, which is already emerging in the EU, the UK and Africa, which would result in delay, uncertainty, and higher costs in the sector.

Em Fenton (they/them), Senior Director of Climate Diplomacy at Opportunity Green, says: “The levels of ambition in the Net-Zero Framework have survived the first week of negotiations at the International Maritime Organization, but may not ultimately survive unscathed – with further compromise on the horizon. It is essential that Member States stand with courage in solidarity with the climate-vulnerable states whose very existence is threatened by a poor outcome at the IMO. Weakened ambition serves no one, it abandons developing countries and overlooks a genuine opportunity to deliver an economically-responsible maritime transition that’s fair for all. Member States must adopt the most ambitious outcome possible and accelerate a global maritime transition that leaves no country behind.”

Lukas Leppert, President of the Clean Shipping Coalition, said: “After some IMO member states continued to launch attacks on climate ambition this week, the Marine Environment Protection Committee must turn things around. Next week, climate leaders within IMO member states have the singular opportunity of translating the IMO GHG Strategy into action – they must stand shoulder to shoulder, ignore distraction from false solutions and establish a global framework that meets shipping’s obligation to clean-up its climate warming emissions in a manner that leaves no state behind.”

Angie Farrah-Thibault, Vice President, Global Transportation at Environmental Defense Fund, said: “The momentum at the IMO is real. While differences remain, Member States have been constructively building a blueprint for a maritime energy transition. Next week, they have the opportunity to turn that progress into action by adopting a binding global framework that gives industry the certainty to invest and deliver cleaner, more energy-secure and fairer shipping for everyone.”

Fanny Devaux, Director, Shipping (Brussels, EU), T&E, said: “It is encouraging to see delegations engaging intensively, but dialogue must translate into concrete results next week. A deal is not an end in itself, it must be measured by its ability to deliver real emission cuts, not by how far governments compromise to protect fossil fuel interests.”

Jamie Yates, Climate and Renewable Energy Manager, Pacific Environment, said: “We are heartened to see constructive engagement from all parties this week, as well as the continued development of an economic element as a critical component of the package. Next week will be the true test if climate ambition can survive compromise and whether any agreement will drive real change. Shipping needs a clear, strong framework to move towards net-zero and truly zero emissions. We urge member states to come refreshed to MEPC 85 ready to close the deal and move the industry off of fossil fuels and the sector towards a just and equitable transition.”

Christiaan De Beukelaer, Senior Lecturer, University of Melbourne, said: “What the world needs is a proverbial horse-strength dose of antibiotics, to be able to withstand the climate crisis. This week, while most wanted to start administering a cure as soon as possible, petro-states, once again, tried to fool everyone into believing that a homeopathic dose is it. The NZF is nowhere near the ambition needed, but adopting anything weaker will simply lock in fossil LNG, thereby strengthening the disease all IMO member states have committed to eliminating.”

Alisa Kreynes, Director of Ports and Shipping at C40 Cities, said, “The agreed Net-Zero Framework is an important basis for a just transition to cleaner shipping, but it is already a compromise. At the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) MEPC 85, Member States must preserve the elements agreed in April 2025, including the fuel intensity standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism, and avoid weakening them further. Especially after the disappointing outcomes of COP31, the shipping sector must maintain high ambition to stay within the 1.5°C limit in the Paris Agreement, while delivering fair support and tangible benefits to vulnerable countries and port communities.”

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: Will the IMO follow the COP-out in Türkiye?
summary: The IMO's GHG Working Group mirrors the recent COP31 collapse, with fossil fuel interests actively obstructing progress on robust climate action. This ongoing stagnation gravely threatens a genuine transition away from high-emitting HFO, perpetuating an unsustainable carbon intensity for the global fleet. Without immediate, decisive policy, the industry will continue its greenwashing while actual CO2 emissions remain unchecked.
content:
The IMO’s emissions talks have resumed in London in the shadow of COP31’s collapse, and informal efforts at a compromise have yet to win broad support.

The world’s climate negotiators left the UN’s COP31 summit in Antalya without a final political agreement after negotiations ran deep into overtime. Countries could not agree on language addressing fossil fuels or climate finance. Oil- and gas-producing nations opposed explicit references to transitioning away from fossil fuels, while the EU, Pacific island nations and others refused to accept a weaker text.

“It was the first time since 2009 that COP had failed like this. It was also the right outcome when petrostates once again stood in the way of progress for everyone,” the Climate Reality Project said.

Transport & Environment said the breakdown showed that fossil fuel interests remain a major obstacle to climate action. COP28’s final text in 2023 called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, but fossil-producing countries have blocked similar language at later COPs despite the growing economic and social costs of climate change, it said.

For the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework, this feels like a bad omen.

The IMO’s GHG Working Group (ISWG-GHG) is meeting in London this week, ahead of the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session (MEPC 85) next week. A possible resumption of the extraordinary MEPC session on 4 December could put the fate of the NZF back on the table.

Davina Hurt, climate policy director at Pacific Environment, sees an uncomfortable parallel between the COP31 and the IMO negotiations.

“The demand for perfection has become a recipe for stagnation. That doesn’t mean lowering our ambition. It means exactly the opposite and acting on it now,” she said. “COP31 showed us what happens when delay wins. The IMO doesn’t have to repeat it.”

Compromise remains elusive

The IMO’s negotiations are hardly starting from a blank page. The NZF’s draft language was approved in 2025, but opposition from the US and several other countries has complicated efforts to move it forward.

An informal group of countries, dubbed the “Risotto Group”, had been exploring a possible compromise ahead of MEPC 85, as first reported by Lloyd’s List.

The group included Saudi Arabia, the US, Brazil, Japan, Singapore, Denmark, Norway, Germany, Greece, the Marshall Islands and Solomon Islands. Other European countries were also understood to have participated.

But the discussions have yet to produce a compromise with broad support, two sources told ENGINE.

“The formal negotiations within the IMO have been complemented by ongoing informal discussions between member states. Various delegations have come together on equal terms without anyone taking the lead,” one source told ENGINE.

“These discussions have allowed member state concerns to be considered, but as far as we have seen, none of the alternative proposals proved more effective or gathered broader support than the NZF does,” the source added. “If anything, discussions have served to highlight the virtues of the NZF.”

A second source told ENGINE that the group had produced a compromise document, but it failed to attract significant support.

China’s position could now prove particularly important.

“China plays a critical role in the negotiations, especially after the absence of the US in international climate policy,” the first source said.

The second source was more direct: “China could be instrumental in securing the framework. It is more important that they don’t block or undermine [the existing version of the text].”

Meanwhile, informal diplomacy continues alongside the official proceedings.

The International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) hosted a reception for delegates on Monday following the first day of ISWG-GHG 23 deliberations, according to former IMO official and IBIA representative to the IMO Edmund Hughes.

“[It is] important to allow delegates to meet ‘informally’ in the margins of these meetings to exchange views and seek to identify where, if any, compromises can be identified and taken forward,” Hughes added.

Pacific Island nations and delegates from the Micronesian Center for Sustainable Transport (MCST) have also been attending informal sessions on the sidelines of the ISWG-GHG discussions, according to MCST researcher John Taukave, who described their participation as “encouraging” for the negotiations.

Some member states are willing to compromise on certain elements of the technical global fuel standard, but significant disagreements remain over the economic measures, Rhona Macdonald, IMO liaison officer at the International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH), said at the end of the fourth day of negotiations.

The disagreements centre on future compliance mechanisms and whether to establish an IMO net-zero fund to manage revenues generated by the measures, she added.

Another test of multilateralism

Four environmental groups have urged Panama’s President José Raúl Mulino to carry the country’s position at COP31 into the IMO negotiations.

In a letter dated 25 November, the Clean Shipping Coalition, Environmental Defense Fund, Pacific Environment and WWF International praised Panama’s support for transitioning away from fossil fuels at COP31 and called on its government to back stronger global shipping emissions regulations at the IMO.

“The outcomes of COP31 highlight the persistent gap between global climate commitments and the ambition required to address the climate crisis,” Malawi’s alternate permanent representative to the IMO, Elias Tsokalida, said, calling for “constructive dialogue and international cooperation” to bridge differences.

“This may be a marathon, but hopefully not a sprint! The Polish delegation is well prepared, and our EU coordination is strong and united under the Irish Presidency,” Poland’s permanent representative to the IMO, Marcin Białek, said.

In other alt fuels news this week, ships able to run on LNG, methanol or ammonia would account for 21% of the annual energy demand of liner shipping, meaning container ships and vehicle carriers, by around 2030, up from 9.8% today, the World Shipping Council (WSC) said in a report.

The Clean Port Coalition, an alliance of industry and environmental groups, has asked the European Commission to set shore power targets for ports beyond 2030 when it reviews the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR). The coalition made the request in a letter to officials in the Commission’s transport and energy departments.

title: Countdown: Setting the stage for the IMO Energy Efficiency Framework discussions at MEPC 85
summary: The IMO's Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) is under fire at MEPC 85, with its current calculation obscuring true propulsion efficiency by including all non-propulsion fuel consumption. While a "propulsion-based CII" is proposed to isolate fuel for movement, this risks creating another selective metric rather than demanding full accountability. True transparency requires a strengthened SEEMP that rigorously manages *all* fuel consumption, ensuring ships are penalized for their total CO2 output, not just a convenient subset.
content:
The big picture

• The Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and Part III of the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) are both operational measures in the IMO Energy Efficiency Framework. Now in its fourth year of implementation, the CII remains under review.

• MEPC 85 (November-December 2026) is an opportunity to make these measures more effective. Of the 21 energy efficiency submissions to MEPC 85, 19 concern the CII, with proposals ranging from correction factors to a full redesign.

• The current CII divides a ship’s total annual CO2 by a proxy for transport work (capacity × distance sailed). Because the numerator includes all fuel consumption, the rating is affected by factors unrelated to the ship’s efficiency in converting fuel into movement – for example, cargo heating or cooling needs.

• In this edition of Countdown Energy Efficiency, we explain a proposal for a propulsion-based CII metric jointly developed by the Center and our knowledge partner, the Royal Institution of Naval Architects (RINA). By including only fuel used for propulsion at sea in the metric, better CII ratings are clearly linked to propulsion efficiency. The propulsion CII then acts as an indicator for propulsion at sea, while a strengthened SEEMP manages all of the ship’s fuel consumption, supported by a framework for planning, logging, and auditing energy efficiency measures.

Why this matters

As part of the IMO’s Energy Efficiency Framework, the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and Part III of the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) entered into force in January 2023. After nearly four years of implementation, a clearer picture is emerging of where the CII falls short. Addressing these shortcomings through multiple correction factors and exclusions can distort the metric and change relative rankings between ships. Over time, it becomes hard to say what the CII measures and what it does not.

Instead of a patchwork of fixes, the Energy Efficiency Framework needs a systems approach: a CII metric more consistently proportional to transport work, backed by a framework that manages efficiency as a whole. Phase 2 of the IMO’s review is the chance to build one.

How the current CII works

The CII of an individual ship is calculated as the ratio of the total mass of CO2 the ship emits over a calendar year to the capacity-based transport work it performs in the same period. Ships are rated A-E (best-worst) depending on their calculated CII.

The numerator in the CII simply counts every tonne of CO2 the ship produces in the year. In fact, these CO2 emissions fall into distinct groups (Figure 1). At sea, emissions are generated by the main engine propelling the ship forward, alongside the auxiliary engines and boilers covering electrical and cargo demand. Outside the sea passage, emissions come from fuel burned while maneuvering, waiting at anchor, approaching a berth, and working cargo in port (Figure 1). Propulsion accounts for the overall largest share of emissions.

The CII’s denominator is a proxy for transport work: the ship’s capacity multiplied by the distance it sails in the year. A poor CII rating is meant to flag an inefficient ship: one that emits too much CO2 for the transport work it delivers. Yet, because the metric groups all emissions together, the CII rating is affected by factors unrelated to how well a ship converts fuel into movement – for example, waiting time at berth, cargo-related emissions, and auxiliary power demands.

This means that two ships with identical propulsion performance can achieve different CII ratings, and a ship can improve its CII rating without becoming any more energy efficient. For example, a ship that spends long periods waiting at anchor or at berth burns fuel without adding to its distance sailed, so its rating worsens even if its propulsion is efficient. Similarly, a ship on short voyages with frequent port calls spends a larger share of its fuel on maneuvering and port operations, which penalizes its rating compared with a similar ship on longer routes.

Without a metric that can reliably distinguish an energy-efficient operation from an inefficient one, it’s challenging for shipping companies to understand how they can improve vessel efficiency, and for regulators to effectively enforce energy efficiency standards.

Introducing the propulsion CII

For the past three years, the Center and RINA have been developing a proposal for a “propulsion CII”, first submitted in document MEPC 82/6/20. The proposed solution is a dedicated metric defined similarly to the current CII (CO2 over capacity-based transport work), but counting only the fuel consumed by the main engine during the sea passage.

Our analysis shows that this metric better correlates with engine load, and therefore with fuel use. The metric makes it easier to identify that a ship rated D or E is using more fuel than similar vessels to perform the same transport work within that ship segment. To improve the rating, the shipowner then looks at propulsion-related factors such as operating speed, hull and propeller condition, and engine performance.

Figure 2 shows data from around 53,000 container ship voyages in 2024. Under the current CII (left), which uses a total Annual Efficiency Ratio (AER) metric, the curves for different lower speeds overlap. Because lower speed acts as a proxy for main engine load, the graph shows that a voyage at low engine load can show a similar or worse total AER – and thus CII rating – than one at high engine load. Without separately analyzing all other fuel use, an operator cannot tell whether a low CII rating comes from propulsion.

Using the propulsion CII (right), propulsion AER rises with engine load consistently across ship sizes. This makes the effect of speed and engine load directly visible in the rating. A worse rating points straight to propulsion, so the operator knows where to act.

A propulsion metric also simplifies the regulation. Voyage adjustments and correction factors can bring the current CII closer to a propulsion metric, but they apply unevenly: for example, container ships and tankers can exclude part of the fuel used for cargo cooling, cargo heating, or discharge pumps, while bulk carriers have no equivalent.

Finally, a propulsion metric is more transparent. It allows industry actors to more directly infer that improved CII ratings are caused by ships using less fuel for propulsion per unit of transport work.

What about non-propulsion emissions?

A propulsion CII covers the largest share of a ship’s fuel consumption (Figure 1), but the rest cannot be left unregulated.

Furthermore, the diversity of non-propulsion fuel consumers on board means that these systems would benefit from more tailored regulation:

• Some onboard systems have a relatively constant load, while others are more variable or intermittent

• Discharge pumps on tankers, ballast pumps, and ballast treatment systems may vary with the number of cargo discharges or ballast operations

• Some systems, such as ventilation and machinery cooling, may be sensitive to air and water temperature

• Some loads, such as cargo heating, are cargo-dependent

Non-propulsion fuel is typically around 20% of a ship’s total consumption, split across several independent systems. Broadly speaking, each of these systems accounts for perhaps 10–20% of the non-propulsion fuel consumption, so roughly 2–4% of the ship’s total. Improving one of those systems by 5% has an effect on total fuel consumption in the order of 0.1–0.2%: smaller than the normal variation in non-propulsion consumption, and well below what an aggregated metric can detect.

HFO = heavy fuel oil

Using real-world data, we also tested several potential energy-efficiency metrics to see if we could find a correlation with use of specific fuel consumers (e.g., discharge pumps). The metrics included gCO2/kWh (specific fuel oil consumption), CO2/h, total CO2, and combinations of these. None showed a consistent pattern like the one between engine load and CII rating as shown in Figure 2. In other words, we could not find a CII-style ratio metric that reliably reflects the efficiency (and achieved improvement) of these onboard systems.

Leaving non-propulsion emissions out of the CII metric does not entail removing them from the regulatory framework. In our proposal, these emissions continue to be reported through the IMO Data Collection System (DCS), and they are managed where they can actually be targeted: in the SEEMP.

Building a stronger SEEMP framework

The SEEMP has the basic principles required for energy efficiency management. However, the feedback loops linking planning to implementation, monitoring, review, and accountability are currently weakly defined in the regulations.

Our proposal with RINA therefore aims to strengthen these feedback loops by changing how the CII and the SEEMP work together. Our SEEMP proposal works in four steps:

Step 1 – Developing the Implementation Plan

The company develops an Implementation Plan, which would consist of pre-defined categories of measures to be taken to improve the ship’s energy efficiency. These measures would relate to both propulsion and non-propulsion fuel consumption, crew training, fouling management, etc. Unlike current practice, the planned measures must then be implemented and evidenced (see Step 2).

The flag administration or a recognized organization (RO) reviews the plan and issues a Confirmation of Compliance (CoC).

Step 2 – Plan implementation and logging

Data is then collected. Every energy efficiency action taken (e.g., hull cleaning, trim optimization, or crew training) according to the implementation plan is recorded, with evidence, in an Energy Efficiency Implementation Log (EEIL). This brings together the information a company holds for each ship and creates a record of implementation that can be used for internal reviews and external audits. Making the EEIL electronic would avoid cumbersome processes of logging and attaching evidence on paper.

The EEIL provides evidence of implementation. In addition, required internal reviews during the implementation year evaluate whether measures should be continued, adjusted, or replaced. Together, the EEIL and reviews show continuous improvement more reliably than the CII alone.

Step 3 – Reporting and verification

The DCS data and the EEIL are then sent to the RO for verification. The RO checks the documentation against the Implementation Plan to assess whether the ship has hit its target and whether the log matches the plan.

The flag administration or RO acting on its behalf then issues a Statement of Compliance alongside the vessel’s CII rating: clean or with reservations. Audits can be triggered by a poor CII rating (D or E) or by persistent mismatches between the implementation plan and the EEIL – on one ship or across a company’s fleet.

Step 4 – Auditing by flag administration or authorized RO (where required)

Audits focus on reviewing a company’s processes, documentation of internal reviews, and EEIL records, as well as interviewing the shore personnel. The outcome of an audit could be a clean pass, a fail, or result in observations and non-conformities to be addressed.

This framework is held together by a continuous feedback loop: the Implementation Plan states what will be done, the EEIL logs what was done, verification compares the two, and the audit examines whether the company’s own processes are in place and being used. The proposal also introduces a designated person ashore (DPA) responsible for energy efficiency. This should not be the same as the DPA for the ISM Code, since the responsibilities and qualifications are different.

Under this system, operational energy efficiency is no longer a number reported once a year, but a management system that a company must evidence and demonstrate in an audit. A SEEMP that is genuinely in use becomes part of a ship’s licence to operate. Our proposal takes what industry frontrunners already do and formalizes it into a regulatory framework to support more efficient operations for the global fleet.

What comes next: energy efficiency on the agenda at MEPC 85

At MEPC 85 (November-December 2026), the Center and RINA’s proposal will be considered alongside several other proposals for revising the CII and the IMO Energy Efficiency Framework. Many of the proposals also aim to make the CII more accurate and more representative of how ships operate, using varying approaches.

title: With Uncertainty Shrouding UN Shipping Climate Talks, NGOs Call on Governments to Avoid Backsliding on Ambition
summary: Ahead of MEPC 85, the IMO's already insufficient Net-Zero Framework faces further sabotage from the US and petrostates, threatening any meaningful reduction in shipping's carbon intensity. Despite the unanimous 2023 GHG Strategy, current backsliding risks maintaining reliance on high-carbon fuels and avoiding stricter FuelEU Maritime-style regulations globally. This continued political inaction ensures the dirtiest ships will evade accountability, allowing excessive HFO usage and exceeding CII ratings with impunity.
content:
Ahead of next week’s meeting of the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85, Nov 30-Dec 4), the Clean Shipping Coalition calls on member states to stay true to the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, by ensuring that the strategy’s ambition and commitment to a just & equitable energy transition are translated into an effective framework.

The IMO’s climate ambition came under severe threat during this week’s meeting of the IMO’s Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23 Nov 23-27). Following four days of mostly closed door discussions, indications suggest that pressure from the US and a slew of petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, is threatening the possibility of a fit-for-purpose IMO shipping climate deal. The levels of ambition of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), the IMO’s already approved mechanism for reducing shipping emissions from shipping, are being questioned and weakened.

“After some IMO member states continued to launch attacks on climate ambition this week, the Marine Environment Protection Committee must turn things around”, said Lukas Leppert, President of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “Next week, climate leaders within IMO member states have the singular opportunity of translating the IMO GHG Strategy into action – they must stand shoulder to shoulder, ignore distraction from false solutions and establish a global framework that meets shipping’s obligation to clean-up its climate warming emissions in a manner that leaves no state behind.”

“IMO member states must match the ambition they unanimously agreed to in the IMO’s 2023 GHG strategy; reduce the climate impact of global shipping, which makes up 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, support the uptake of sustainable marine fuels and technologies, agree a financing mechanism for decarbonisation of the sector, and to deliver on a just and equitable energy transition, so that vulnerable countries facing disproportionate impacts are supported in the transition”, added Leppert.

Earlier this week, the Clean Shipping Coalition wrote to José Raúl Mulino Quintero, President of the Republic of Panama, commending Panama’s strong position at COP31, and urging Panama to take a similarly strong stance at the International Maritime Organization.

“Next week, Panama must join others by bringing their COP31 climate leadership to the IMO, by helping ensure the UN’s shipping body enshrines the importance of climate regulation and a just & equitable transition in IMO’s global shipping policies”, said John Maggs, the Clean Shipping Coalition’s Representative at IMO.

“Communities on the frontlines of the climate crisis are fighting for their survival”, said Andrew Dumbrille, Co-Director of Equal Routes. “A global climate framework for shipping must centre their rights and support their economies. The just and equitable transition that IMO Member States committed to in the 2023 GHG Strategy cannot remain a promise on paper. It needs to be put into practice to support those most impacted by the climate crisis and who have done the least to cause it. There can be no compromise on this.”

“An ambitious global framework for reduction of shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions would establish a level playing field that reduces emissions and drives production of sustainable technologies and fuels”, said Sönke Diesener, Senior Policy Officer Maritime Transport at NABU. “Instead, a framework weak in ambition and impact rises will result in a fragmentation of shipping’s climate regulation with a multitude of national and regional regulations filling the gaps. IMO member states should deliver on the chance of harmonized regulation of shipping’s climate heating emissions instead of fragmentation.”

“The lack of progress this week shows that many countries are unwilling to accept proposals that would lower ambition or put the IMO’s GHG strategy goals out of reach; shipping cannot afford more delays in tackling its climate pollution”, said Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director at Ocean Conservancy. “When negotiations resume next week, IMO member states must come prepared to deliver a strong framework that cuts emissions, provides industry certainty and funds for a transition for the countries most at risk. There is simply too much at stake to keep kicking the can down the road.”

“After drawn-out discussions and slow progress, it is more important than ever to recall the climate goals of the IMO and its member states”, said Felix Klann, Shipping Policy Officer at T&E. “If IMO member states cannot deliver on their obligations, additional action is needed to fill the gaps, not only on setting targets, but in providing incentives and investments in clean fuels and technologies.”

title: Pacific Environment and City of Yokohama sign MOU to advance zero-emission shipping and port decarbonization
summary: Pacific Environment and the City of Yokohama signed an MOU for a five-year "zero-emission shipping" framework. Such frameworks are common; dirtiestships.com awaits verifiable reductions in HFO consumption and improved CII ratings, not just collaborative intentions. Until tangible cuts to carbon intensity are demonstrated, this remains another greenwashing exercise.
content:
21

Five-year cooperation framework establishes opportunities for collaboration on green shipping corridors, vessel decarbonization, clean maritime energy and marine environmental protectionMr. Yasuhiro Shimbo of the Port and Harbor Bureau of Yokohama and Grace Healy of Pacific Environment

(Photo credit: Pacific Environment)

YOKOHAMA (November 27, 2026) — On November 25, 2026, Pacific Environment, an international environmental organization headquartered in San Francisco, and the City of Yokohama’s Port and Harbor Bureau signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to establish a framework for cooperation to accelerate the transition to zero-emission shipping and ports in Japan, across Asia, and globally.

The MOU was signed by Mr. Yasuhiro Shimbo, Director General of the Port and Harbor Bureau of the City of Yokohama, and Grace Healy, Head of Programs at Pacific Environment, at OXExpo (Ocean Transformation Exhibition) 2026 in Yokohama, Japan.

[Read the signed Memorandum of Understanding between the City of Yokohama and Pacific Environment.]

Mr. Yasuhiro Shimbo, Director General of the Port and Harbor Bureau of the City of Yokohama, said:

“International cooperation and the exchange of expertise are essential to accelerating port decarbonization and the transition to sustainable shipping and ports. Today’s MOU with Pacific Environment provides an important platform for strengthening our efforts to decarbonize the Port of Yokohama and enhance its competitiveness as an international port. By drawing on Pacific Environment’s international experience and expertise, we hope to identify new opportunities and practical solutions to advance our Carbon Neutral Port initiatives.”

Grace Healy, Head of Programs at Pacific Environment, said:

“We are honored to formalize our partnership with the City of Yokohama. This MOU provides an important framework for bringing together Yokohama’s experience as a leading international port and Pacific Environment’s worldwide network and policy and technical expertise. We look forward to working together on green shipping corridors, zero-emission shipping, the protection of marine ecosystems and the well-being of port communities throughout the Pacific region.”

The five-year MOU establishes a framework for the two organizations to explore opportunities for collaboration in six areas, ranging from the decarbonization of vessels and the development of green shipping corridors to clean maritime energy, international maritime policy, marine environmental protection, and capacity building for port workers and communities.

Through this partnership, the two parties intend to exchange expertise, consult on research initiatives, develop policy recommendations and organize joint workshops, seminars and conferences to advance shared objectives in shipping and port decarbonization.

The City of Yokohama has been advancing its Carbon Neutral Port (CNP) initiatives with the goal of achieving carbon neutrality at the Port of Yokohama by 2050. In March 2025, the Yokohama municipal government formulated the Port and Harbor Decarbonization Plan for the Port of Yokohama, which won the 2025 IAPH Sustainability Award for Climate and Energy, setting out a comprehensive approach to reducing greenhouse gas emissions across the port and surrounding waterfront industrial areas.

The City of Yokohama has also made progress through initiatives such as next-generation marine fuel bunkering, the development of its CNP Sustainable Finance Framework and collaboration with private-sector companies on renewable energy and other decarbonization projects.

Pacific Environment, an international environmental organization with consultative status at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) since 2011, works across the Pacific Rim to protect critical ecosystems, reduce pollution and advance solutions to the climate and biodiversity crises. Through its international engagement and partnerships with governments, port authorities, research institutions and civil society organizations, Pacific Environment works to accelerate the transition to zero-emission shipping and sustainable ports.

title: India and Denmark explore ammonia ship engines and shore power for ports
summary: India and Denmark merely discussed future ammonia engine development and port electrification, offering little immediate relief for current carbon intensity failures. While Everllence's ammonia dual-fuel engines see initial installation, these are distant solutions for a global fleet still overwhelmingly burning heavy fuel oil. Copenhagen's shore power for *cruise vessels* offers marginal emission reductions, conveniently side-stepping the urgent need for electrification among high-polluting cargo ships.
content:
India and Denmark explored cooperation on ammonia-fuelled marine engines, port electrification and alternative-fuel bunkering during an Indian ministerial visit to Copenhagen on 23 and 24 November 2026. Shantanu Thakur, India’s Minister of State for Ports, Shipping and Waterways, led a delegation of government officials and representatives from the Indian shipbuilding and ports sectors. The visit paired talks with engine developer Everllence with a review of Copenhagen’s shore power infrastructure.

India examines ammonia engines at Everllence

The delegation met Everllence’s leadership and technical teams to discuss the development and use of two-stroke marine engines capable of running on ammonia. The talks put propulsion technology and fuel infrastructure on the same agenda. For shipowners considering ammonia-fuelled vessels, the availability of bunkering infrastructure will help determine where those ships can operate on the fuel.

A separate project shows how the technology is moving into ship construction. Earlier in November, the first Everllence ammonia dual-fuel main engine for Höegh Autoliners’ Aurora-class programme was lifted into a car carrier under construction in Jiangsu, China. The engine installation is part of Höegh’s fleet programme. India’s talks with Everllence focused on examining the technology and opportunities for cooperation.

Copenhagen visit puts shore power and green bunkering in focus

At the Port of Copenhagen, Thakur met Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt, Denmark’s Minister for Urban and Rural Affairs and Transport. The delegation visited the shore power installation and discussed how Danish ports manage electrification, plan bunkering facilities for alternative marine fuels and integrate clean energy into terminal operations.

Copenhagen inaugurated its shore power facility for cruise vessels at Oceankaj in June 2025. Onshore power supply allows compatible ships to draw electricity from land while berthed and switch off auxiliary engines used to generate onboard power. This can reduce exhaust emissions and engine noise at the berth.

Indian ports are also moving ahead with shore power. Separately from the Denmark visit, Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority awarded a ₹76.92 crore contract to Leena Powertech Engineers for a shore power project at Gateway Terminals India.

Green shipping corridor work builds on the bilateral partnership

Maritime cooperation forms part of the India–Denmark Green Strategic Partnership, launched in 2020. The two countries established the Indo-Danish Centre of Excellence on Green Shipping in 2025 to support technical cooperation on maritime decarbonisation. Its remit includes green shipbuilding, port digitalisation, seafarer training and sustainable ship recycling.

The countries also launched a pre-feasibility study on green shipping corridors in India in 2025. A 2026 workshop brought together the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, the Directorate General of Shipping and the Indian Ports Association to advance collaboration on potential corridor projects. The Copenhagen meetings added discussions with an engine developer and a port operator to that ongoing work.

FAQs

What did India and Denmark discuss during the Copenhagen visit?

The delegation examined ammonia-fuelled marine engines at Everllence and discussed shore power, port electrification and alternative-fuel bunkering at the Port of Copenhagen.

How does shore power reduce emissions at ports?

It lets compatible vessels connect to land-based electricity at berth and switch off auxiliary engines used for onboard power, reducing local exhaust emissions and noise.

What stage has India–Denmark green shipping corridor cooperation reached?

The two countries launched a pre-feasibility study in 2025 and held a workshop in 2026 to develop cooperation on potential corridor projects.

title: Moment of truth for maritime industry at London meet
summary: The IMO faces another critical vote on ship emissions, years after a vital carbon pricing mechanism was stalled by political obstruction from the US and oil-exporting nations. This proposed levy, designed to charge vessels for emissions exceeding an acceptable threshold, is crucial for tackling carbon intensity and penalizing excessive HFO consumption, akin to FuelEU Maritime fines. Without such a robust economic component, the industry's "decarbonisation" remains hollow greenwashing, allowing the dirtiest ships to continue polluting with minimal financial consequence.
content:
LONDON – The International Maritime Organization (IMO) will meet in London in late November and early December to vote on a plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions from ships after US President Donald Trump forced its postponement in 2025.

The London-based organisation, a United Nations body that governs shipping, supported a global pricing system in April 2025 to help curb the use of pollutants such as carbon dioxide and methane.

The IMO’s 176 member states later gathered in October 2025 for a vote on formally adopting the plan. But it never took place after Trump, a climate change sceptic, threatened sanctions against countries voting in favour.

The proposal also faced pressure from major oil-exporting nations Saudi Arabia and Russia.

What is at stake this time?

Whether member states stick to the same proposals is unclear.

In 2025, they considered measures that would see highly polluting vessels gradually reduce emissions starting in 2028, with the ultimate aim of achieving total decarbonisation by around 2050.

An economic component to the Net Zero Framework (NZF), which ultimately sank 2025’s formal vote, was designed to incentivise the industry to rapidly reduce its emissions.

It proposed charging vessels for emissions that exceed a certain threshold, with the proceeds intended to fund rewards for low-emission ships and provide financial support for the transition of countries vulnerable to climate change.

Why is the measure contested?

Trump – a proponent of fossil fuels who has reversed climate-related policies since returning to the White House – urged a vote against the IMO plan in 2025 via his social media platform Truth Social.

“The United States will NOT stand for this Global Green New Scam Tax on Shipping,” he stated at the time.

Unlike Washington, Gulf delegations and Russia theoretically support the principle of decarbonising the sector, yet cite potential negative economic impacts as grounds for their opposition.

For its part, the maritime industry is calling for a “practical, effective and fit-for-purpose” regulatory framework, while urging that consideration be given to the costs of alternatives to polluting fuels.

That position was outlined in a statement in November released by the world’s leading commercial shipping associations.

What to expect this time around?

The economic component of the NZF is particularly at risk, as it is the measure facing the strongest opposition from the US and other major oil-producing nations.

A maritime source close to the matter told AFP that “the industry is highly sceptical of the IMO’s ability to manage global financial flows, and fears that it could end up being more of a global financial burden than a catalyst for decarbonising”.

Speaking to AFP, IMO chief Arsenio Dominguez said he felt “confident that member states will continue to work together constructively to deliver on the commitments we collectively made” regarding greenhouse gases.

Arne Rasmussen, chief analyst at Global Risk Management, noted that “a substantially watered-down agreement now appears more realistic”.

On Nov 22 , the UN climate conference COP31 ended in failure as negotiations on a pact collapsed following a row over fossil fuels.

“This highlights the difficulties of reaching international climate agreements and is hardly an encouraging sign for the IMO negotiations resuming on Nov 30 ,” Rasmussen added. AFP

title: Regulatory Change, Digital Transformation and Decarbonization Take Center Stage at the 40th Hellenic Marine Technical Committee

Such discussions often prioritize compliance strategies and perceived efficiency gains over tangible, absolute emission reductions, allowing continued high carbon intensity despite looming FuelEU Maritime fines.
