title: Interferry: UK should learn from the EU’s Maritime ETS experiences
summary: Interferry warns the UK against repeating the EU's Emissions Trading System (ETS) failures, where collected revenues largely prop up national budgets instead of funding genuine decarbonization. This fiscal sleight of hand constitutes pure greenwashing, forcing the ferry sector to pay approximately €1 billion annually without adequate support for critical emissions reduction investments. Such diverted funds perpetuate reliance on high-carbon fuels, demonstrably failing to drive the urgent transition to cleaner shipping.
content:
Following the 20 November EU-UK Summit, Interferry, the association representing the ferry industry worldwide, warns against using maritime ETS revenues to prop up national budgets instead of funding the sector’s green transition.

Interferry welcomes the ambition to harmonize rules between the European Union and the United Kingdom following the EU-UK Summit on 20 November. However, the association urges the UK government not to repeat the mistakes made during the rollout of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) for maritime transport.

“The UK must take note of Europe’s harsh awakening and resist the temptation to casually add maritime ETS revenues to its national treasury. Up until now, EU ETS funds have largely been used to prop up national budgets rather than support actual decarbonization. While the ferry sector is well aware of its role to facilitate the decarbonization of maritime transport, drawing large amounts of money from the sector and expecting it to be self-sufficient in financing current and future decarbonization is misguided, much as the rest of Europe has recently realized”, said Johan Roos, Interferry’s Director of Regulatory Affairs and added:

“The implementation of the EU ETS was done in three phases, somewhat softening the substantial financial blow on operators. The UK should mirror this approach.”

In their 20 November Joint Statement, EU and UK leaders welcomed the conclusion of negotiations to link their respective Emissions Trading Systems – an agreement aimed to take effect from 2028 that will allow mutual recognition of allowances and exempt goods from respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms. While regulatory alignment is a positive step toward reducing trade friction, Interferry stresses that the EU is currently working to undo significant economic damage that the EU ETS has inflicted on intra-EU trade.

Under the current European framework, the ferry sector alone is obliged to pay approximately 1 billion Euro per year into the system. During the on-going revision of the EU ETS, there seems to be strong support from most stakeholders that money collected from the maritime sector should be put to use to support the decarbonization of that sector, e.g. through subsidies for green fuels and proliferation of high-capacity charging points for all-electric ships – primarily ferries.

Interferry’s warning echoes concerns raised by the UK Chamber of Shipping in connection with the 20 November reset talks. The Chamber emphasized that shipping serves as the vital physical link between the UK and its largest trading partner, warning that unaligned or purely punitive ETS compliance costs ultimately pass through to UK imports, exports, supply chains, and consumers.

title: Econowind turns ten as maritime players turn to wind
summary: Econowind celebrates a decade and 170 VentoFoil sales, yet this announcement provides no concrete, verifiable data on actual CO2 reductions or improved vessel efficiency. We demand transparent, vessel-specific data demonstrating significant fuel oil consumption (FOC) reductions and consistent improvements in Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) scores to avoid FuelEU Maritime fines. Until wind-assisted propulsion translates into measurable, substantial cuts in HFO usage and lower carbon emissions across entire fleets, such initiatives risk remaining mere greenwashing.
content:
From wooden prototypes on a car roof to more than 170 VentoFoil units sold, the Dutch wind-assisted ship propulsion (WASP) specialist looks back on a decade of practical engineering and a changing industry.

Econowind is celebrating its tenth anniversary, with more than 170 VentoFoil units sold to shipping companies around the world. Reaching the ten-year mark highlights both the company’s journey from early start-up to established scale-up, and a broader shift in how global commercial shipping views wind power.

When founder Frank Nieuwenhuis launched Econowind in 2016 in collaboration with ship design firm Conoship International, many in the maritime sector were still sceptical about wind-assisted ship propulsion, so he set out to show that compact, vertical wings could cut a cargo ship’s fuel use. His first tests were very hands-on: he bolted wooden prototypes to the roof of his car and used a vacuum cleaner to mimic the suction that keeps air flowing smoothly over the wing. Later, he tested an early prototype on a car trailer.

Early pioneers did not just have to sell a new technology, they had to sell wind itself as a credible modern energy source. When early setbacks tested Nieuwenhuis’ resolve, Gavin Allwright of the International Windship Association (IWSA) persuaded him to persevere.

Taking the concept to sea was not smooth, as early trials required manual operation by an onboard technician, and showed that smaller wings delivered limited savings on larger ships. Econowind responded by developing automated bridge controls that respond to changing winds. It also added tilting designs, so crews can lower the wings during cargo handling or heavy weather. That engineering work laid the foundation for the 3-series VentoFoil, the company’s best-selling unit.

Over the past ten years, Econowind has grown alongside the wider WASP market. What began as a handful of trial installations is now a recognised commercial segment, with installations roughly doubling every twelve months.

“In terms of the number of vessels installed, Econowind is right in the front line, definitely one of the frontrunners,” says Gavin Allwright, Secretary General of the IWSA.

“What has changed most over the past decade is perception: shipping now sees wind not as a romantic throwback, but as a 21st-century toolbox of commercial solutions.”

Much of that growth comes down to cost and pressure to act. With fuel accounting for around half of a ship’s operating expenses, shipping companies and charterers are facing high and unpredictable fuel prices, alongside the heavy cost of long-term decarbonisation. Alternative fuels such as green methanol and ammonia remain expensive, and the production and bunkering networks they require are still being built. Meanwhile, rules such as the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and FuelEU Maritime, which grants a reward factor for wind propulsion and allows operators to pool compliance surpluses, are turning emissions reduction into a direct financial case.

VentoFoils ease the load on a ship’s main engine, giving operators a practical way to reduce fuel burn and compliance costs without relying on new fuel supply chains that are still taking shape. Wind propulsion also works well alongside hull and voyage optimisation as well as future low-carbon fuels.

Looking back on the past decade, Nieuwenhuis says: “This journey has been full of trials and learning by doing. It would not have been possible without the people behind Econowind and everyone who supported us along the way.”

To mark the anniversary, Econowind is launching a series of ten stories, each told by a different voice. Together, clients, shipyards, and other maritime stakeholders tell the story of how both the company and commercial wind propulsion have developed over the decade.

Entering its second decade, Econowind is focused on expanding its manufacturing capacity and rolling out the 30-metre steel 5-series VentoFoil for deepsea fleets. Ten years after testing its first scale models, the company aims to help make wind assistance a standard part of life at sea.

“Wind propulsion is approaching an inflection point. The groundwork has been laid by technology providers such as Econowind, and the sector is now absolutely ready to ride the wave,” Allwright adds.

title: Mitsubishi Shipbuilding to Supply MAmmoSS® Ammonia Fuel Handling System– For Four Vessels Set to Become Japan’s First Ammonia-Fueled Car Carriers
summary: Mitsubishi Shipbuilding will supply ammonia fuel systems for four car carriers, yet these "decarbonization" vessels won't sail until 2030, offering no immediate carbon intensity improvements. While praising ammonia for zero CO2 at combustion, this announcement conveniently ignores the significant environmental burden of grey ammonia production and its toxic handling risks. Such distant plans are a classic greenwashing tactic, distracting from the urgent need for current fleets to reduce HFO consumption and meet immediate FuelEU Maritime targets.
content:
Mitsubishi Shipbuilding Co., Ltd., a part of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) Group, has been selected to supply its MAmmoSS® ammonia fuel handling system(Note) for four ammonia-fueled car carriers to be built under a construction and operation project announced at a joint press conference held on October 27, 2026.

Seven companies are jointly undertaking the project: Imabari Shipbuilding Co., Ltd., Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, Ltd., Kyokuyo Shipyard Corporation, JERA Co., Inc., Shin Kurushima Dockyard Co., Ltd., Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha, and Nihon Shipyard Co., Ltd. The four vessels are scheduled for completion in 2030 as Japan’s first ammonia-fueled car carriers. The supply of MAmmoSS forms part of the seven-company ammonia fuel supply chain project. The project is the world’s first initiative to integrate ammonia fuel procurement, supply, and vessel operations.

MAmmoSS, which Mitsubishi Shipbuilding will supply, safely and reliably supplies ammonia stored in fuel tanks to the engines. The system also incorporates equipment that neutralizes toxic surplus ammonia, as well as a range of safety features including an emergency shutdown function, making it an essential part of ammonia-fueled vessels. Mitsubishi Shipbuilding will also be responsible for undertaking the basic design of the vessels’ ammonia fuel tanks.

Because ammonia emits no CO2 when burned, it is considered a promising next-generation fuel option for achieving decarbonization in international marine transport. Mitsubishi Shipbuilding will leverage the technologies and expertise it has developed in the field of gas fuel supply systems to supply ammonia fuel supply systems that deliver both safety and reliability, thereby contributing to the commercial deployment of vessels powered by next-generation fuels and the decarbonization of the maritime industry.

title: New Center framework turns sustainability risk into a decision-making tool
summary: A new "sustainability framework" from The Center proposes to help shipping lines de-risk future fuel investments beyond basic carbon metrics. This initiative prioritizes corporate reputation and long-term financial exposure, rather than immediate, verifiable reductions in HFO consumption or carbon intensity. Until tangible cuts in CO2 emissions are demonstrated and FuelEU Maritime compliance is met, such frameworks risk becoming another layer of greenwashing.
content:
For years, decarbonization decisions centered on two questions: is it technically feasible, and is it economically viable? Today, a third question is becoming just as important: is it sustainable beyond the carbon?

Sustainability isn’t only about reducing greenhouse gas emissions. As shipping moves towards a multi-fuel future, each fuel choice carries its own risks: resource availability, shifting regulations, reputational exposure, and pressure from stakeholders.

A fuel that works at pilot scale, in one region, under one regulatory regime, may not hold as it scales.

Left unmanaged, these risks can undermine even a long-term decarbonization strategy with solid technical and economic foundations.

The risks you don’t see coming

Many sustainability risks sit upstream in a fuel’s value chain: in feedstock production, energy sourcing, land use, and third-party certification integrity. Companies buying the fuel have little direct control, but they can still be held accountable when something goes wrong.

Without early visibility, a company can lock into a fuel pathway that later proves reputationally, socially, or commercially indefensible. A fuel can pass every test on cost and feasibility and still carry very different risks depending on its origin and supplier.

By surfacing these risks before capital is committed, the Center’s Sustainability Framework can help companies decide which low-emissions fuels to invest in.

As sustainability requirements across shipping tighten, from fuel certification to emissions accounting, early assessment of which fuel pathways will remain compliant let companies secure long-term supply with confidence.

Introducing the Center’s Sustainability Framework

The framework is built on earth system science, the Center’s understanding of a just and equitable transition, and a holistic approach to decarbonization that looks beyond carbon alone. It translates planetary boundaries and social and socioeconomic criteria based on recent discussion at the IMO into 14 practical sustainability dimensions, grouped as:

Importantly, these sustainability dimensions are interrelated. A fuel that cuts emissions can increase pressure on land or water, while another can deliver benefits well beyond carbon. The framework maps these connections across the whole value chain, so leadership teams can compare options and see trade-offs before their fuel choices are locked in.

In practice, the framework delivers three things:

• The right conversation: Sustainability, procurement, and strategy teams work from the same picture. The framework enables informed discussions of synergies and trade-offs and supports decisions based on a shared understanding.

• Synergies as well as risks: Decarbonization investments often bring co-benefits that go unrecorded, from local jobs to improved land management. The framework brings these into view, so the business case reflects the full value of a decision.

• Levers for action: The framework helps identify trade-offs and highlights where they can be addressed or mitigated along the value chain. It also supports the definition of minimum sustainability thresholds when assessing suppliers.

The Sustainability Framework in practice

Together with our strategic partner Hapag-Lloyd and its decarbonization team, we ran five real-world fuel pathways through the Sustainability Framework:

• Ammonia

• Biomethane

• Cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL)

• Fatty acid methyl esters (FAME, also known as biodiesel)

• Very low-sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO)

Each fuel was assessed across the same sustainability dimensions, giving Hapag-Lloyd a single, comparable view of risk across fundamentally different fuel types. As the potential fuel buyer, Hapag-Lloyd provided data on current and potential suppliers and led the assessment of the available fuel options. The Center supported the analysis by providing the assessment framework and LCA expertise, including a high-level review of the risks associated with each fuel.

With line of sight across the value chain, the buyer can select the best-positioned supplier for each fuel pathway. Factors like how a supplier sources feedstock, manages land and water use, and treats the communities and workers in its value chain sit alongside price and volume.

When we took a closer look at FAME, at first glance all the assessed suppliers looked equally strong on emissions reductions. But the framework made it visible that one supplier’s feedstock carried substantial food security and freshwater risks, while the others’ did not. Same fuel, very different exposure.

Arne Maibohm, Director Decarbonization, Hapag-Lloyd AG

The view from Hapag-Lloyd

Hapag-Lloyd’s sustainability team found the framework highly useful, supporting the assessment of future fuels while also prompting a reassessment of fuels already in use, looking beyond carbon intensity alone.

The framework enhanced the questions we must ask, not only about the fuels we plan to use, but about the ones we use today. Better data will be available as the industry matures, and the companies that start enhancing their questions now will be the ones best prepared for it.

Choosing the right fuel is no longer only about carbon. It is about better understanding all elements of sustainability in the full value chain behind the fuel. The framework gave us that perspective and showed that transparency is something the whole industry has to build together, with suppliers as partners.

Arne Maibohm, Director Decarbonization, Hapag-Lloyd AG

Three lessons learned from the framework pilot

Data input

Supplier sustainability certificates are the most reliable source today, but they mostly cover carbon intensity. For the other dimensions, future users should expect to rely on estimates from life-cycle studies and academic research, with differing units and boundaries. Social risks, assessed by reviewing media coverage for controversies, proved easier to quantify than expected.

Visualization

With reliable data, results are simple to visualize. The team is now evaluating where to set the thresholds for each risk level.

Communication with external parties

Responses are often slow and incomplete, given the complexity of supply chains and the many traders between producer and buyer. Short, precise questions work best to obtain a direct answer, and stricter requirements can be set for new suppliers.

As the industry matures, the Hapag-Lloyd sustainability team expects data transparency to improve. Until then, working with the Center makes the difference: the method, the reference data, and the experience of a first full pilot.

Next steps: rolling out the framework to new users

The Hapag-Lloyd pilot is the first in a series. The Center is now opening the Sustainability Framework and its underlying model to the wider maritime industry. With tools like this framework, sustainability risk can move from a niche concern to a standard part of how the sector makes decarbonization decisions.

title: Global patchwork of shipping decarbonization rules looms after COP31 collapse, warns PortXchange
summary: The IMO's repeated failure to adopt a global Net-Zero Framework, obstructed by a few nations, guarantees prolonged reliance on high-carbon fuels. This regulatory paralysis directly fuels a surge in conventional-only vessel orders, now 61% of the orderbook, locking in excessive future CO2 emissions. Shipping lines now face a costly, fragmented regulatory patchwork, increasing their exposure to FuelEU Maritime non-compliance fines and higher carbon intensity ratings.
content:
Maritime emissions tracking and reducing specialist PortXchange has warned that shipping is heading for a costly patchwork of national and regional climate rules unless International Maritime Organization (IMO) member states adopt the Net-Zero Framework next week, after the UN climate summit in Antalya collapsed without a deal.

COP31 closed on 22 November without a final text, the first time since 2009 the annual summit has failed to agree, after Saudi Arabia and other oil producers forced fossil fuel language out of the draft. Eight days later, IMO member states meet for MEPC 85 (30 November to 3 December), with the resumed extraordinary session on 4 December expected to decide the framework’s fate. The last attempt, in October 2025, was postponed by 57 votes to 49 after the United States threatened tariffs, visa restrictions and port fees against countries backing the framework.

“COP and the IMO are watching the same film,” said Sjoerd de Jager, Managing Director and Co-Founder of PortXchange. “A handful of countries whose economies run on oil and gas are blocking what most of the world has already said it wants. At COP they deleted the words. At the IMO, they went further and threatened the trade of anyone who voted the other way.”

The delay is already costing the transition. The UCL Energy Institute and Getting to Zero Coalition’s Climate action in shipping 2026 report calls last year’s failure to adopt the framework “the single most transition-regressive event” in its five years of tracking. The share of tonnage on order that can run on scalable zero-emission fuels fell from 9.5% to 5.7%, while conventional-only ships rose from 54% to 61% of the orderbook. Even if it is adopted next week, the framework cannot take effect before 2029.

The Global Maritime Forum counts 84 active green shipping corridors worldwide, yet only four have reached the stage where vessels, infrastructure or fuel plants are actually being built or operated. The cost gap between conventional and low-carbon fuels is the main brake.

“Nobody on the water is short of ambition. Owners are electrifying barges, trailing hydrogen-derived fuels and asking the IMO, again and again, for clear rules,” said de Jager. “What kills most corridors between pilot and operation is the operating cost: someone has to pay the premium on green fuel and electricity. The Net-Zero Framework is the only measure on the table built to close that gap worldwide and a few governments are holding it back while the rest of the industry pays for it.”

Without a global deal, countries and regions will keep writing their own rules. The EU already applies its ETS and FuelEU Maritime to ships, and the Netherlands and Spain have added national obligations on marine fuel suppliers. Since July, the UK has run a separate carbon price, the UK ETS, on domestic voyages and on emissions while ships of 5,000 GT and above are in UK ports. Every extra layer adds compliance work for operators trading across borders and pushes cost and cargo from one market to the next. The UK Chamber of Shipping has asked for any extension of the UK ETS to international voyages to wait until the IMO completes its Net-Zero Framework negotiations, so the December 4 decision will also shape how far that patchwork spreads in UK waters.

“If member states walk away again on 4 December, the IMO’s authority as shipping’s global regulator takes a hit it may not recover from,” said de Jager. “What replaces it is a patchwork of regional carbon prices and fuel rules and ships cross every border, so this industry will pay for that fragmentation more than any other.”

PortXchange is urging ports and operators to act whatever the vote. Synchronizing arrivals so ships slow down at sea instead of waiting at anchor cuts fuel burn straight away. At the Port of Algeciras, real-time port call coordination through PortXchange’s Synchronizer cut idle time per vessel arrival and departure by nearly 40% and avoided an average of 32.9 tonnes of CO2 per port call. Measuring emissions call by call with EmissionInsider then shows where shore power and other investments will make the biggest difference.

“Member states have one job on 4 December: adopt the framework as it stands,” de Jager said. “Another year of delay is a decision too and the industry will remember who took it.”

title: VIEWPOINT: Biofuels and the Future of Energy in Shipping — Ship & Bunker
summary: The maritime industry's "strategic priority" for a diversified energy mix often serves as an excuse to prolong reliance on high-carbon fuels. Discussions of future fuel flexibility ring hollow while current carbon intensity remains excessive and many vessels fail their CII ratings. Without immediate, concrete transitions away from HFO, this indecision only guarantees escalating FuelEU Maritime fines, not genuine decarbonization.
content:
The maritime industry is beginning to make decisions that will shape its energy mix for decades to come. Responsible for transporting approximately 90% of global trade, the sector faces the challenge of reducing emissions without compromising the efficiency and reliability of its operations. The transition has already seen significant technological advances and commercial developments, but uncertainty remains over which alternatives will achieve scale and competitiveness.

Trade disputes between major economies, international conflicts, and growing concerns over energy security have begun to directly influence global supply chains. Trade routes may shift, markets may impose restrictions, and energy sources once considered secure may lose their competitiveness or availability. For an industry that operates globally and makes investments with time horizons spanning several decades, maintaining a range of supply options has become a strategic priority.

The very nature of shipping favors a diversified energy mix. Vessels with different characteristics, routes spanning multiple regions, and fuel availability that varies from port to port make it unlikely that a single fuel will dominate. This diversity could provide greater operational flexibility and allow different solutions to advance according to their competitiveness and availability.

Available technologies are at different stages of development. Some use fuels that have been commercially produced for decades and can make use of some of the existing infrastructure. Others require new industrial facilities, distribution systems, and vessel modifications. These differences affect not only costs but also how quickly each alternative can achieve commercial scale.

For shipowners, the ability to operate on different fuels helps preserve options as market conditions and environmental requirements evolve. Vessels built today may undergo successive technological and regulatory changes. Fuel flexibility helps reduce risks and maintain competitiveness over a vessel's service life.

The economic implications of these choices extend beyond the purchase price of fuel. Energy content, engine efficiency, retrofit investments, and logistics costs through delivery to the vessel must all be considered. A fuel that appears cheaper may not be the most economical option when all these factors are taken into account.

Environmental performance adds another dimension to the analysis. Reducing maritime emissions can also benefit producers, exporters, and consumers seeking to lower the carbon footprint of their supply chains. For these benefits to translate into economic value, reliable mechanisms for certification, traceability, and recognition of avoided emissions will be needed. Developing these mechanisms could help reward lower-carbon solutions and distribute their costs among the various participants in international trade.

Regulation will play an important role in this process. Transparent criteria for assessing lifecycle emissions, applied in a technology-neutral manner, will allow alternatives to be compared based on their actual performance. Regulatory stability will also be essential to guide investment decisions and encourage the development of new supply chains.

However, a fuel's viability cannot be established solely on the basis of its technical or environmental characteristics. Shipping depends on tightly scheduled operations in which safety, reliability, and availability are essential. Moving from isolated trials to recurring commercial contracts therefore represents an important milestone. It is at this stage that an alternative fuel begins to demonstrate its ability to become part of the maritime industry's day-to-day operations.

Bioethanol provides a concrete example of this progress. Advances in engine technologies capable of using alcohol-based fuels, along with the introduction of regular commercial operations, are opening up new opportunities for an already established industry. Its competitiveness is supported by Maritime Forecast to 2050, a study published in 2026 by DNV, one of the world's leading ship classification and certification organizations. By comparing the potential availability and emissions abatement costs of different marine fuels, the study identifies sugarcane-based bioethanol as one of the lowest-cost options for reducing carbon emissions in shipping. Its adoption is expected to expand initially along routes with favorable production, bunkering, and demand conditions.

Brazil has significant advantages that position it to participate in this market. Decades of experience in biofuel production and use, industrial scale, technological development, and logistics infrastructure provide a strong foundation. However, these strengths alone do not guarantee competitiveness. The country will need to demonstrate its ability to ensure reliable supply, competitive costs, and internationally recognized environmental performance.

The energy transition in shipping is likely to be driven by a combination of solutions capable of meeting different operational, economic, and environmental needs. In this emerging market, biofuels could play a significant role, particularly where established supply chains can accelerate adoption under competitive conditions. For Brazil, which is already participating in this transition, an opportunity is emerging to bring its expertise in renewable fuels to a new frontier of the global energy market.

title: IMO Sounds Alarm Over Shortage of Training Berths for Future Seafarers
summary: The IMO flags a critical shortage of training berths for seafarers, exposing a fundamental disconnect in an industry quick to trumpet "green" initiatives but slow to invest in its human capital. This systemic failure to provide essential onboard experience directly impacts operational efficiency and safety, crucial factors in managing actual emissions. Until shipping lines prioritize foundational issues like proper training over mere PR, their commitment to genuine decarbonization remains highly questionable.
content:
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling on shipping companies to make more training berths available to cadets, highlighting a longstanding disconnect between the industry’s need for qualified seafarers and the lack of opportunities for young people to gain the sea time required to enter the profession.

In many developing countries, aspiring officers complete their shore-based maritime education only to spend years waiting for an onboard training placement, even as shipping companies struggle to recruit qualified personnel.

In an announcement Tuesday, the IMO outlined efforts to expand its NextWave Seafarers initiative, which aims to address the bottleneck through cooperation between governments, shipowners and maritime training institutions.

More than 80 participants representing over 25 countries gathered at IMO headquarters in London on November 20 to formally launch the second phase of the initiative and explore ways to increase the availability of onboard training opportunities.

The program’s pilot phase, developed in partnership with Saudi Arabia’s Transport General Authority and national shipping company Bahri, saw 19 cadets from developing island nations and least developed countries complete their onboard training aboard Bahri vessels.

The second phase aims to train at least 30 additional cadets, with women accounting for half of participants. The IMO also wants to recruit at least five shipping companies to provide training berths, laying the groundwork for a wider international partnership.

The workshop examined practical barriers to cadet placements, including visa restrictions complicating crew changes, as well as the importance of providing a safe and supportive working environment for young seafarers entering the industry.

The shortage of training berths exposes a fundamental challenge in addressing the industry’s workforce needs. Expanding maritime education alone will do little to increase the supply of qualified officers if graduates cannot secure the mandatory sea time needed to earn their professional credentials.

Without sufficient participation from shipowners, the industry risks leaving a pool of prospective seafarers untapped at a time when it needs to attract and retain the next generation of maritime professionals.

title: CMA CGM's Saadé concedes 2050 net zero target is out of reach
summary: CMA CGM CEO Rodolphe Saadé now admits his company's 2050 net-zero target is "unrealistic," exposing the hollowness of their previous ambitious decarbonisation rhetoric. Despite committing $30 billion to primarily LNG and methanol dual-fuel newbuilds, Saadé blames geopolitical factors and slow alternative fuel development for this failure. This concession highlights the continued reliance on fossil-derived fuels and the significant uphill battle for genuine emissions reductions across their massive 700-vessel fleet.
content:
One of shipping’s most vocal proponents of decarbonisation has conceded that its 2050 net zero ambitions are unlikely to be realised, just days ahead of crucial environmental negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

Speaking at the Assises de l’économie de la mer in Montpellier yesterday, CMA CGM chairman and CEO Rodolphe Saadé put the investment required to decarbonise global shipping at more than $1trn.

“We must be realistic: under current circumstances, we will not be able to meet our targets by 2050,” Saadé said.

The French shipping magnate cited geopolitical conflicts lengthening voyages and driving up operating costs, the absence of a unified international regulatory framework and the slow development of low-carbon fuels.

CMA CGM has already committed nearly $30bn to LNG- and methanol-powered newbuilds, with more than 200 dual-fuel vessels scheduled to be in its fleet by 2030. The Marseille-headquartered carrier operates more than 700 containerships, of which over 400 are owned.

The admission comes ahead of next Monday’s opening of the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting in London, where member states will attempt to overcome divisions surrounding the proposed Net-Zero Framework.<

Saadé also expressed concern about the future of the French flag, criticising recurring uncertainty surrounding France’s tonnage tax regime. He stressed that containership investments typically involve commitments spanning 25 years, while employing French petty officers adds €2m annually to a ship’s operating costs. According to Saadé, tonnage tax regimes cover 86% of the global fleet and are in place in 22 European countries. In September, CMA CGM dropped plans to register seven large newbuilds under the French flag, citing additional taxation.

title: UK and EU aim to link emissions trading schemes by January 2028
summary: Shipping lines can anticipate simpler paperwork by January 2028 as the UK and EU aim to link their Emissions Trading Schemes. This inter-scheme allowance trading, however, does not alter the fundamental flaw: 50% of international voyage emissions for vessels over 5,000 GT remain only partially addressed. Such distant deadlines and incomplete coverage allow continued reliance on high-carbon fuels, delaying real decarbonisation for the persistent fleet of 'dirty ships'.
content:
The UK and EU have agreed to link their emissions trading systems, targeting 1 January 2028 for the arrangement to take effect alongside the UK's planned expansion of carbon pricing to international shipping.

IMAGE: Flags of the UK and the EU. Getty Images

The agreement could simplify compliance for shipping companies operating under both schemes by allowing them to use UK and EU carbon allowances interchangeably, the UK's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in an explainer on 20 November.

Under the planned expansion, the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) is set to cover 50% of emissions from international voyages between UK and non-UK ports for vessels of 5,000 GT and above from 1 January 2028.

The UK ETS has already covered 100% of emissions from domestic voyages and emissions at berth in UK ports since 1 July 2026.

The EU ETS similarly covers 50% of emissions from voyages between EU and non-EU ports, while requiring shipping companies to account for all emissions on voyages between EU ports.

The UK ETS will also adopt the EU's approach to neighbouring container transhipment ports. Ports on the European Commission's designated list will not count as UK ports of call when determining which voyage emissions fall under the scheme. The list is updated every two years.

Once linked, the two schemes will continue operating separately but allow shipping companies to use allowances from either market to meet their emissions obligations.

This could eliminate the need for operators covered by both schemes to purchase UK allowances (UKAs) and EU allowances (EUAs) separately.

The arrangement is also intended to cover emissions obligations for 2027, with the first deadline for using allowances interchangeably scheduled for 30 September 2028.

The UK and EU are also working towards a common administrative process that could allow shipping companies to manage compliance under both schemes together.

The UK also plans to remove its minimum auction price for carbon allowances when the link takes effect.

Impact on shipping

The agreement aims to bring UK ETS shipping rules more closely in line with those of the EU ETS, including requirements for monitoring, reporting and verifying emissions.

The UK plans to end the temporary arrangement that allows shipping companies to surrender allowances for only 50% of emissions on voyages between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

These voyages are expected to face the full 100% requirement from 2028, bringing them in line with other domestic UK routes.

Meanwhile, passenger and ro-pax vessels serving islands with fewer than 200,000 residents and no road or rail connection to the mainland are expected to qualify for a temporary surrender derogation until at least 31 December 2030.

Ice-class vessels are also set to qualify for a 5% reduction in their allowance surrender obligations until at least the same date.

The agreement also addresses how shipping companies can account for lower-emission fuels.

Operators would be able to apply a zero-emission factor to eligible biofuels, renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) and recycled carbon fuels, provided they meet the sustainability and greenhouse gas savings requirements under the EU Renewable Energy Directive.

The UK government has also said it will review how its carbon pricing rules interact with any future global emissions measure adopted by the IMO. The review would aim to avoid charging shipping companies twice for the same emissions while keeping compliance requirements manageable.

“Any review would take into account any relevant changes to the EU ETS, and its outcomes will maintain support for maritime decarbonisation, and remain consistent with net zero,” the department said.

The UK and EU are working towards bringing the two carbon markets together by January 2028, with technical preparations and legislative approvals still required.

By Konica Bhatt

title: B100 Cheaper Than Gasoil in ARA, but Owners "Can't Get the Approval" to Lift It: KPI OceanConnect — Ship & Bunker
summary: Despite pure B100 biodiesel trading $150/tonne below gasoil in ARA, shipping owners are reportedly refusing its uptake, citing engine warranty concerns. This refusal persists even with substantial EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime savings, making the economic case for B100 "literally zero argument" against gasoil. Such inaction reveals a profound disconnect between decarbonization rhetoric and operational commitment, prioritising perceived risk over tangible emissions reductions and financial prudence.
content:
B100 in ARA has been trading about $150/mt below gasoil, with subsidies, in mid-October

"Literally zero argument" for gasoil once ETS and FuelEU savings are added, says KPI OceanConnect's Jesper Sørensen

Lead buyers say they "can't get the approval"; engine warranties the sticking point

Early-2026 dip put down to the first FuelEU cycle and an uptick expected as the 2026 deadline nears

Biofuel now available at more than 220 ports

Pure biodiesel is now trading below gasoil in the ARA hub and there is no economic argument left for not lifting it, but bunker buyers are still being refused approval by their owners, according to KPI OceanConnect.

"As late as yesterday I received an email from our supplier in Europe pointing out that B100 in ARA, with subsidies, is trading $150 below gasoil," Jesper Sørensen, global head of alternative fuels and carbon markets at KPI OceanConnect, told Ship & Bunker in an interview at SIBCON in Singapore last month.

"There's literally zero argument for using gasoil versus biofuel, because by using the biofuel, one, you're getting a cheaper product, even energy adjusted," he said.

"Then you take into account the savings you have on ETS and the surplus that you inevitably will build on FuelEU Maritime. The case speaks for itself."

Conventional fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the Middle East conflict while biofuel prices have moved far less, he said, and the premium has narrowed as a result.

Earlier this year Sørensen told Ship & Bunker that buyers were missing the boat on those narrowing premiums.

With the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) now covering 100% of shipping emissions and a conversion factor of about 3.2 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of fuel, the allowance saving alone is worth around $320/mt, he said.

"There is no premium if you are saving $320 a ton. It's pretty much as simple as that."

Indeed, Sørensen said one KPI OceanConnect customer at the conference told him he is "banking money every time I lift B100”.

Proof of Concept

Price is usually the key driver for bunker buyers, so the natural question to ask when biofuel prices are so favourable is why demand is not higher.

“I asked one customer why they were not lifting B100 FAME that meets ISO 8217:2024 specifications and he said, I can't get the approval to do so," he said.

"I actually thought we were past that stage when it came to biofuel. I understand there's still a feedstock discussion, but we should be beyond proof of concept."

The approvals in question are from engine manufacturers, and the issue behind them is warranties, Sørensen explained.

"If you have a ship owner, they of course want to protect their assets,” he added.

Of course, not all ports have biofuel priced as favourably as ARA, and how much an owner gains from lifting biofuel still depends on their specific voyage and ports of call.

Still, taken as a whole, and once compliance costs are counted, "the economics globally have spoken in favour of using biofuels," he said.

"Maybe what we need right now is for those ship owners who actually do take advantage of this to come out and share the experience, because those using bio tell me they have nothing but positive things to say."

The Dip

Sørensen puts the fall in biofuel volumes this year down to the mechanics of FuelEU Maritime's first compliance cycle rather than any loss of interest.

Owners who used biofuel to cover 2025 had burned it by December, and those who had not could no longer use it for that year, so from January 2026 attention turned to the paperwork for the first compliance year, he said.

"Verifying, collecting documents, submitting them, getting them approved, and then finding out, what is my obligation, what have I covered, what have I not covered," he said, with that work running up to the April deadline.

Some owners who had bought biofuel "solely for the sake of complying," rather than to decarbonise, also found they had taken more than their 2025 obligation needed, and have cut back this year as a result, he said.

"We are coming towards crunch time, so if you want to comply with 2026, then fuel needs to be ordered and it needs to be burned," he said.

"We expect, and we hope, that there will be an uptick in demand now."

If that demand does come, buyers will be pleased to learn that availability is no longer the constraint either.

title: Tresco Group acquires Green Maritime and sets course for seagoing shipping
summary: Antwerp-based Tresco has acquired "Green Maritime," a firm providing operational data from 220 short-sea vessels, claiming to offer precise fuel consumption measurements. This acquisition directly targets the escalating regulatory pressure from EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, where accurate data is now essential for compliance and avoiding substantial fines. However, merely tracking emissions does not inherently force a reduction in actual carbon intensity or a necessary shift away from excessive high-carbon fuel consumption.
content:
Tresco, the Antwerp-based leader in inland navigation software backed by Strada Partners, has acquired Green Maritime, the Dutch specialist in operational data on board seagoing vessels. Green Maritime’s technology runs on 220 vessels today, mainly in short sea shipping. The deal takes Tresco beyond inland waterways into the much larger seagoing market, where EU climate rules are driving demand for measured fuel and emissions data. It is the next step in Tresco’s ambition to build a broad maritime technology group, through organic growth and targeted acquisitions.

Measured data, straight from on board

Green Maritime collects on-board data on fuel consumption, engine performance and navigation. Shipowners use it to report emissions, cut fuel costs, spot technical problems early and run their fleets more efficiently. The system is affordable and quick to install. Instead of calculating with bunker delivery notes and estimates, it measures what a ship actually burns. Proven in daily operation on 220 vessels, it is ready to scale.

Former sea captain Bart Schut founded Green Maritime in 2020, after seven years at sea and five years running operations at a shipping company. He built the platform around the problems he ran into on board and in the office.

Regulation drives demand

Since 2024, seagoing vessels of 5,000 GT and above fall under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The scheme is being phased in: for emissions from 2026 onwards, shipowners must surrender allowances for 100% of their verified emissions. FuelEU Maritime has applied since 1 January 2025 and lowers the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used on board step by step. By the end of 2026, the European Commission will assess whether to extend the rules to smaller ships, which could bring short sea vessels and coasters below 5,000 GT into scope.

Both systems rest on accurate measurement. A shipowner who doesn’t know what a ship burns can’t report its emissions correctly, let alone reduce them. The same data keeps fuel costs in check and shows how a fleet performs, so the investment pays off well beyond compliance.

“Regulation is driving innovation in the maritime sector,” said Evert Bulcke, CEO of Tresco Group. “The rules are mostly European, but their impact reaches far beyond Europe. Emissions reporting is only as good as the operational data underneath it. That sounds simpler than it is: a ship is not a car. It’s a complex system.”

Building a broad maritime technology group

Tresco equips some 9,000 vessels in European inland shipping with navigation and automation software. Green Maritime opens up a much larger market: thousands of short sea vessels will need emissions monitoring and better operational data in the coming years. Over time, Tresco will bring its inland and seagoing data together on one platform, giving customers a single view of their fleet on inland waterways and at sea.

“Green Maritime gives us a strong position in seagoing shipping, with a product that has proven itself on 220 vessels,” said Bulcke. “The value in maritime technology lies in reliable data on board, a strong market share and deep knowledge of the sector. You don’t copy that with AI. We see room to double the number of connected vessels, and that’s before we look at Southeast Asia.”

Matthias Vandepitte, Managing Partner at Strada Partners and Board Member at Tresco Group: “When we invested in Tresco in 2024, the plan was clear: build on its leadership in inland navigation to create a broad maritime technology group. Green Maritime fits that plan perfectly, with proven technology, a founder who knows the sector from the bridge, and a market that regulation is opening up fast. We’re excited to back Evert and Bart in this next chapter.”

What changes for customers

Green Maritime will remain a separate business unit, led from Apeldoorn by founder and CEO Bart Schut. Seagoing shipping has its own market, language and way of working, so integration will happen step by step. The full team is joining. Existing customers keep their contacts and their service, and gain access to Tresco’s European installation and dealer network and to the group’s R&D capacity.

title: Wind sails, e-methanol and a stalled global deal: Can hard-to-decarbonise shipping go green?
summary: The IMO is again attempting a "Net-Zero Framework" for shipping, years after political interference stalled a global deal, ensuring prolonged reliance on high-carbon fuels. While discussing wind sails and e-methanol, the continued industry embrace of LNG—a fossil fuel—exposes a lack of commitment to genuine decarbonisation. This delayed action guarantees continued excessive HFO usage, escalating carbon intensity, and ensures ships will continue to exceed CII ratings, incurring significant FuelEU Maritime fines.
content:
A year after Trump stalled a global net-zero shipping deal, the IMO is trying again – with wind power, batteries, e-fuels and LNG in the mix.

Last year, the Trump administration derailed a global breakthrough aimed at cleaning up shipping, one of the world’s most difficult-to-decarbonise sectors. Now the International Maritime Organization (IMO) is trying again.

Between 23 November and 4 December, the UN agency will meet to discuss the sector’s future Net-Zero Framework. The decisions made will lock in the emissions profile of ships for the next 20+ years.

A framework including a global fuel standard and a pricing mechanism on greenhouse gas emissions from ships was already approved by IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee in spring 2025. It was scheduled for formal adoption in October 2025 – until the POTUS threatened to impose tariffs on all countries that supported it, leading further talks and decision-making to be postponed by a year.

Is there a fresh chance to get a global deal on shipping by the end of 2026? Could the Democrats’ recent victory in the midterm elections offer new momentum? Or will the Net-Zero Framework run aground once and for all?

Shipping is one of the hardest to abate sectors’

Euronews Earth spoke to stakeholders working towards deep decarbonisation of the sector. While they anticipate stormy weather along the course, there are also a few glimmers of hope on the more distant horizon.

Shipping moves more than 80 per cent of global trade by volume and is responsible for 2.3 per cent of global CO2 emissions, roughly the same as the entire annual emissions of Japan. Promising solutions already exist, but scaling them depends on infrastructure, investment and policy frameworks.

Shipping is one of the hardest to abate sectors”, says Dr Peter Schniering, CEO and co-founder of Future Cleantech Architects (FCA), a science-based non-profit organisation and innovation think tank headquartered in Germany. His colleague, FCA Cleantech Analyst Pauline Leroi, provided much of the data and analysis below.

About 90 per cent of the global shipping fleet runs on oil-based fuels. Tankers, container ships and bulk carriers are “the biggest polluters”, says Leroi, followed by cruise ships and general cargo ships. Together, those five vessel types are responsible for 664 million tonnes of CO2 emissions per year. Europe is responsible for 14 per cent of those shipping emissions (China 17 per cent, USA 9 per cent).

The majority of emissions come from large deep-sea shipping vessels. There are currently around 6,000 container ships sailing the world’s oceans and rivers, 8,200 oil tankers, some 13,000 bulk carriers and 960 ships used for tourism.

Wind assisted propulsion and onboard carbon capture: Tools for net-zero shipping

Leroi unpacks the different pathways to net-zero shipping, from alternative fuels to electrification and efficiency solutions, and explains the trade-offs behind them. Slow steaming would be an efficient first step, in her opinion, especially for container ships: “Steaming 10 per cent slower results in up to 20 per cent less fuel burnt.”

There is no magic nautical treasure map – it looks more like a jigsaw puzzle, combining several solutions that fit well together. “Efficiency improvements – such as better hydrodynamics, smarter logistics, upgraded machinery, digitalisation – can save five to 20 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions,” says Leroi. “Wind assisted propulsion systems and on-board carbon capture could save up to a further 25 per cent of GHG emissions.”

Wind-power assisted propulsion systems, such as rotor sails, suction sails or wing sails, could bring down GHG emissions by up to 30 per cent per nautical mile – if weather and wind conditions are favourable. That is mostly the case on busy transatlantic or transpacific routes: “There’s lots of wind around there, usually,” Leroi says.

However, “that’s not the best solution for container ships”, which already have containers piled up, leaving little room for high-towering systems. “But it would be good for tankers and bulk carriers.”

Some 150 ships already have wind assistance today. For tankers, combining wind assistance with shore power, plugging into the port’s electricity supply instead of running onboard generators while docked, could save up to 70 million tonnes of CO2 per year, Leroi says.

“The biggest GHG reduction, however, could come from changing marine fuels – up to 90 per cent reduction, as well as from new propulsion technologies, up to 100 per cent (battery-electric, battery hybridisation, nuclear)”, Leroi says.

Redesigning shipping ports for an electric future

Regarding electric battery solutions, Leroi is in favour and mentions China, which is already operating a 120-metre-long all-electric container vessel on the Yangtze, the world’s third-longest river. “Specifically smaller cargo vessels should all go electric,” she recommends. In a second wave, shorter and medium distance cargo shipping routes could opt for electric battery systems as well.

Smaller cargo vessels should all go electric. ‘’

Pauline Leroi, Cleantech Analyst, FCA

This needs a container battery swapping system at ports along the ship’s route: instead of bunkering oil or gas, cargo ships take onboard a container packed with batteries. Medium distances could get split, with stopovers enabling vessels to change empty container batteries for fully charged ones.

China leads on swappable container battery systems, but there are start-ups in Europe too. Battery swapping for container ships could save another 35 million tonnes of CO2 per year.

Dual fuel ships could switch from LNG to green alternatives in future

Even without a global IMO deal, a transition will go ahead in the shipping sector anyway, experts agree, albeit at a slower pace. That’s where the European Union steps in. “Let’s take ships running on heavy fuel oil,” Leroi explains: “Under FuelEU Maritime Regulation they will not be compliant by 2030 and European vessels will have to transition to lower carbon emitting fuels.”

“Until green fuels are available at scale, transitional fuels could offer only a limited bridging solution,” Leroi emphasises. “Today, liquefied Natural gas (LNG) is the most mature option” – but still far from perfect. While heavy fuel oil has lifecycle emissions of 92 grams of CO2-equivalent per megajoule, LNG still stands at 76g CO2e/MJ, a 25 per cent reduction. Many EU shipowners have opted for it, as it is compliant under the FuelEU Maritime Regulation and other regulations.

The EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation is currently the only fully working regulatory framework designed specifically to cut shipping emissions. Patrick Cummins-Tripodi, FCA’s Brussels-based Cleantech Policy Officer, calls the EU’s approach “a strong basis for greening the sector”, but points to the “fact that LNG-powered ships comply with the FuelEU Maritime Regulation”: as a result, “LNG continues to dominate the ship orderbook”.

Why is this an issue? “There is significant methane slip during onboard combustion as well as methane leakage during upstream fuel production and transition, which is not always accounted for,” Leroi warns.

EU shipping methane emissions rose by 30 per cent in 2025. That’s alarming considering that methane is around 80 times more potent at trapping heat than CO2 over a 20-year timeframe. Cummins-Tripodi adds that “methane emission values at the EU and IMO level do not account for the full impact of methane slip, which if updated could penalise the choice of LNG”.

Ships ordered today will operate well beyond 2050, so the order books show what shipowners are betting on. 78 per cent of vessel orders are still for conventional oil propulsion systems – almost 2,200 ships designed to run on fossil fuels. If shipowners move away from oil, they mostly opt for LNG (407 vessels ordered), then methanol (134), according to the 2025 order book.

“It is important to add that many of those ordered ships have a dual fuel design,” Leroi flags. Dual fuel ships designed for running on LNG, ‘grey methanol’ or on ‘grey ammonia’ – produced using fossil fuels – can later switch to ‘green methanol’ or ‘green ammonia’, produced using renewable energy sources.

“Being able to burn those alternative fuels does not mean that they necessarily will – some of those vessel types will continue to burn heavy fuel oil.”

Why can’t shipping rely on biofuels or e-fuels?

Why not just switch to biofuels, with lifecycle emissions of just 21g CO2eq/MJ?

“The main issue with biofuels when decarbonising the shipping sector is that the biofuels feedstock availability simply cannot meet the scale of shipping’s fuel demand. And they are three to four times more expensive,” explains Leroi.

And what about e-fuels, such as e-methanol, e-ammonia or liquid green hydrogen? “They can offer very significant reductions (in terms of GHG emissions) – but e-fuels are even six to seven times more expensive than heavy fuel oil, for instance.”

Leroi is sceptical about e-ammonia: “It is highly toxic to fish and the maritime environment in general.” Even so, she says low-carbon ammonia “could really cut a lot of emissions” on the largest bulk carriers and container ships, if toxicity and handling are addressed. On liquid green hydrogen, she points to “the very low energy density”, meaning more tanks would be required for the same energy output.

E-methanol, on the other hand, has the advantage that the propulsion technology works well and the technology readiness level is high. Its lifecycle emissions are low, just 28g CO2eq/MJ. But it still is prohibitively expensive, for the moment, because production is lagging behind.

Using it on cargo ships could cut up to an estimated 320 million tonnes of CO2 per year. Cruise ships could also be hybridised with low-carbon methanol, biomethanol or e-methanol, for a further 40 million tonnes, and Europe has “real leverage”, as 97 per cent of cruise ships are built here.

Why don’t e-fuel suppliers ramp up production?

Addressing the issues with production isn’t so simple: “Fuel producers need to know that vessels will buy green fuels. Ship owners need to know these fuels to be available before they order new vessels. And ports need to build bunkering infrastructure that connects the two,” Leroi explains.

One of those first movers is Knud Erik Andersen, co-founder and CEO of European Energy, a company in sustainable energy generation. It has invested heavily in battery storage, solar and wind power, and in Power-to-X facilities – plants producing sustainable e-fuels using renewable energy sources.

With the recently inaugurated Kasso site in Denmark, European Energy made headlines. It is the world’s first large-scale commercial e-methanol facility, with an annual production capacity of 42,000 tonnes – and operating entirely on solar energy. The plant, next to Northern Europe’s largest solar park, produces e-methanol with up to a 97 per cent reduced carbon footprint compared to fossil-based products.

We need long-term regulatory certainty that Europe sticks to these commitments and ambitions,” says Lars Dyrholm, CEO of the Kasso plant. “We have plans for more plants [but] when you make an investment as large as this, you really need certainty for the future income… No one will make an investment like this unless they are sure that the product produced can compete in the market.”

Andersen has a proposal: “Why shouldn’t the public sector in Europe buy e-fuels for naval ships, for the defence industry? The public sector could not only give support by grants and subsidy schemes, it could also act as a customer.”

Measures such as the sustainable maritime fuel allowances under the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) “may help with the final cost, but it may not solve the chicken-and-egg problem” with supply and demand, Cummins-Tripodi says. Incentives and/or tough legal obligations are needed to ensure that all stakeholders take the necessary steps.

An e-fuel market still needs to be created, production needs to be scaled up globally, and the world is still waiting for a reliable international legal framework from the IMO.

Saving 280 tonnes of CO2 each day per ship

One of the biggest buyers of green methanol produced at Kasso is the Danish logistics group Maersk, which is converting part of its global fleet to sustainable fuels.

The world’s first methanol-enabled cargo ship, the 172-metre Laura Maersk, started service in 2023. This was followed in 2024 by Ane Maersk, a 350-metre container vessel carrying up to 16,000 containers when fully loaded. Compared to a sister ship powered by heavy fuel oil, the Ane Maersk saves 280 tonnes of CO2 per day.

Ten more dual-fuel methanol vessels joined the Maersk fleet in 2025, bringing the company’s total to 19 (out of some 700 vessels). The target for 2030 is 94 dual fuel vessels.

Maersk stresses the importance of global regulation – and deeply regrets the delay of adopting the Net-Zero Framework: “Our climate transition plan is significantly dependent on the regulatory landscape, especially our ability to shift to lower greenhouse gas emission fuels,” the company states. “This signature regulatory framework would lay the foundation for closing the price gap between lower GHG emission fuels and fossil-based fuels.”

Port Esbjerg wants to become an international benchmark for sustainability

At Port Esbjerg, where Denmark borders the North Sea, COO Jesper Bank says: “It’s quite clear for us from a strategic perspective that we have to be able to serve a multi-fuel market. But it is also very clear that this path forward is not clear, because you have many [fuelling] alternatives today.”

“The effort from the political side should not be on the technical issues – we will solve that. But it should be on creating the framework, the conditions for the market to develop,” Bank says.

He also calls for European alignment on hydrogen: “We need coordination of national hydrogen strategies. These are very different today: Sweden has one strategy, Denmark doesn’t really have one and Germany has still another one.”

The regulatory gap extends to ports, says Cummins-Tripodi: “Apart from the EU’s Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation’s loose target for LNG, there is no obligation on ports or fuel suppliers to ensure the supply of alternative fuels.”

Uncertainty is increasing pressure on shipowners

Shipowners are adrift in an ocean of regulatory uncertainty. Some in-depth studies, such as classification society DNV’s 10th Maritime Forecast to 2050, alert that “regulatory uncertainty is increasing pressure on shipowners”.

It stresses the urgent need for “stronger global regulatory signals” that “could accelerate the uptake of energy-efficient measures, enabling the global fleet to consume up to 25 per cent less energy by 2050 compared to a scenario where regulation is driven [only] by regions”.

The global Net-Zero Framework

Getting the global Net-Zero Framework adopted would create a pricing mechanism with set prices on the greenhouse gases ships emit, to encourage the industry to lower emissions to comply with a global fuel standard. It would apply to all oceangoing ships over 5,000 gross tonnage – the vessels responsible for over 85 per cent of global shipping emissions – and IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee would set up a Sustainable Fuel Certification Scheme to make sure fuel emissions and sustainability get independently verified.

If the greenhouse gas fuel intensity is too high, a price has to be paid. If a ship emits below a certain threshold or switches to zero or near-zero emission fuels, it will get financially rewarded. IMO could set up a Net Zero Fund, collecting revenue from non-compliant, heavily polluting ships to reward low-emission ships.

It should not really be called a global carbon tax, the IMO insists. It would be more of a performance-based GHG-intensity target system: vessels that exceed pollution limits must pay tiered compliance fees, while those that outperform can earn tradeable credits and be eligible for rewards.

Cummins-Tripodi isn’t optimistic about the talks. “Last year’s proposal will probably not survive,” he says. “It is highly unlikely.”

The IMO deal to some extent mirrors the EU’s approach, including a greenhouse gas intensity reduction target for shipping, but he warns of a shortcoming: “it could be cheaper for companies to pay penalties instead of complying”.

title: Time Ticking: Two Weeks for Governments to Green-Light Framework for Cutting Shipping Emissions
summary: The IMO convenes again to finalize its Net-Zero Framework, a long-debated proposal still lacking concrete enforcement mechanisms to genuinely curb shipping's rising carbon intensity. Despite calls for urgency from the Clean Shipping Coalition, the framework's actual impact on excessive HFO consumption and carbon intensity targets remains unconvincing given past deferrals and weak alternative proposals. Without robust implementation, this framework risks becoming another greenwashing exercise, failing to prevent ships from exceeding their CII ratings and incurring FuelEU Maritime fines.
content:
As a crucial fortnight of meetings opens at the International Maritime Organization opens in London, the Clean Shipping Coalition calls on member states of the UN’s shipping agency to back adoption without further delay of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) – the UN shipping body’s proposed mechanism for reducing shipping emissions.

Following the IMO’s deferral of a decision on the NZF in October 2025, the upcoming Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23 Nov 23-27) and the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85, Nov 30-Dec 4), provide an opportunity to reaffirm commitment and a platform for adoption for this crucial framework.

“The clock is ticking – IMO member states have just two weeks to protect the global climate from shipping emissions – they must adopt the Net-Zero Framework without further distraction or diversion”, said Lukas Leppert, President of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “IMO member states have already created a greenhouse gas strategy and agreed and approved the regulatory framework to deliver on that strategy – now it’s time to adopt and implement the NZF. The book is closed on further wrangling, it’s time for governments to show courage by taking action now to reduce shipping’s climate heating emissions.”

“The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.”

“Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support”, said Leppert. “These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best and only course ahead.”

“Recent election results have showcased broad support for tackling climate change”, said John Maggs, the Clean Shipping Coalition’s Representative at the IMO. “ Brazil, one of the key architects of the NZF, saw climate a central issue during the presidential elections that saw Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secure a fourth term. Additionally, the blue wave of the US mid-terms could reshape the climate policies of one of the strongest opponents of the NZF. With the impetus for seeking ‘alternative proposals’ apparently fading, countries can now reassess their positions and hopefully stand firm in support of the NZF.”

“IMO Member States must use ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85 to secure adoption of the Net-Zero Framework,” said Andrew Dumbrille, Co-Director of Equal Routes. “Adoption would make well-to-wake GHG fuel intensity requirements mandatory for the first time. To deliver on that promise, the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) Guidelines must fully account for methane slip and upstream methane emissions from LNG. Robust methane accounting is part of how the Framework lays the foundation for a just and equitable transition for those most affected by shipping’s emissions.”

“By adopting a common global framework for the shipping industry – the NZF – the IMO provides a level playing field and enables the ramp-up of sustainable solutions”, said Sönke Diesener, Senior Policy Officer Maritime Transport at NABU. “A clear reduction pathway, including a binding goal for 2040, and financial support for sustainable fuels will provide the planning security required to invest into climate-friendly technologies and fuels. The maritime industry stands ready to decarbonize and is waiting for the IMO’s regulatory signal to get started.”

“Pollution from shipping emissions is dirty and dangerous, causing an estimated 250,000 premature deaths and six million cases of child asthma each year and rivaling major industrialized economies in climate impacts”, said Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director at Ocean Conservancy. “Adopting the agreed upon Net-Zero Framework is the IMO’s quickest and most effective way to protect communities, address climate change, and create certainty for the shipping industry for decades to come.”

“The IMO has an opportunity to put shipping on a credible path to net zero, but ambition without accountability is just words on paper”, added McCullough. “The Net-Zero Framework must deliver meaningful emissions cuts, incentivize truly cleaner fuels, and generate funding to help countries make the transition. We need a deal that closes loopholes, prevents new fossil fuel lock-in and puts the resources behind the promises. As this year’s stunning weather disasters make clear, our ocean and the industry cannot afford to kick the hard decisions down the road again.”

“Three years ago, the IMO promised a just and equitable transition for shipping, leaving no one behind; in the coming days, governments must deliver on that promise by adopting the Net-Zero Framework, with ambitious economic measures at its heart”, said Anaïs Rios, Senior Shipping Policy Officer, Seas At Risk. “There is nothing just or equitable about protecting shipping’s dependence on fossil fuels while passing the costs of climate inaction onto the world’s most vulnerable communities. For countries dependent on imported food, those costs are not abstract. They threaten food security, livelihoods and lives. Over the next fortnight, IMO member states must agree on adoption of the NZF.”

“The biggest danger at MEPC 85 is no longer delay, but a rushed deal that would have shipping reliant on polluting fossil LNG and crop biofuels over real solutions”, said Alex Springer, Deputy Shipping Director at T&E. “IMO member states, including the EU, must resist the pressure from an entrenched minority to reach any deal at the cost of ambition.”

“The IMO must seize this opportunity to transition to clean fuels and eliminate much of the harmful pollution from shipping”, said John Steelman, Deputy Director of Clean Air Task Force’s Transportation Decarbonization program. “To ensure the Net Zero Framework is as effective as it needs to be, it must incentivize the shipping industry to invest in truly low-carbon fuels and engines as well as innovative ship designs and operations.”

• ISWG-GHG-23 IMO Papers from CSC and NGO

• MEPC 85 IMO Papers from CSC and NGO

Background:

The shipping sector makes up 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions – pumping 1 billion tonnes of GHGs into the atmosphere every year, comparable to the world’s fifth biggest emitting country, Japan. The IMO has committed to achieving its GHG Strategy goal, including its long-term goal of decarbonisation by 2050, its interim targets of a 30% reduction in absolute emissions by 2030 and 80% by 2040, and its commitment to a just and equitable transition.

The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.

title: IMO faces tough compromise on shipping emissions rules amid US opposition
